packs.title: First words
packs.blurb: The handful of chunks that get you through a first conversation: greeting someone, saying who you are, and admitting when you are lost.

entries.pattern: Dutch glues the greeting together: goede + morgen. Same for goedemiddag and goedenavond.
entries.hook: One word, not two. If you can say goedemorgen you can say the other three by swapping the time of day.

entries.pattern: A fixed question. Literally 'how goes it', so there is no word for 'you' in it at all.

examples.nl: Hoe gaat het met je moeder?

entries.hook: Learn the four words as one sound. Picking it apart to find 'you' will only confuse you.
entries.pitfall: The reply is `Goed, en met jou?`, not a repeat of the question.

entries.pattern: Does double duty: 'please' when asking, and 'here you are' when handing something over.
entries.hook: Say alstublieft to anyone you would call `u`. The `u` is literally sitting in the middle of the word.
entries.origin: Squashed from `als het u belieft`, 'if it pleases you'. That is why the polite form is alstublieft, with the `u` still visible inside it.

entries.pattern: Three words, always together. The polite version swaps je for u: dank u wel.

examples.nl: Dank je wel voor je hulp.

entries.hook: `bedankt` is the quick everyday version. `dank u wel` is the one for officials.

entries.pattern: `hoor` is a softener with no English translation. It takes the edge off whatever came before it.

examples.nl: Sorry hoor, dat wist ik niet.
examples.en: Sorry about that, I did not know.

entries.hook: Dutch sprinkles `hoor`, `even` and `maar` everywhere to sound friendly. Using one makes you sound far less abrupt.

entries.pattern: A whole verb that exists only for naming yourself. No 'is' and no 'name' in the sentence.

examples.en: My name is Sara. And you?

entries.hook: `heten` means to be called. `Ik heet Sara` is literally 'I am-called Sara'.
entries.pitfall: `Mijn naam is ...` is understood but sounds stiff. Dutch people say `Ik heet ...`.

entries.pattern: `uit` is the fixed preposition for origin. Not `van`.
entries.hook: Pair it with its question. You will be asked `Waar kom je vandaan?` within a minute of meeting anyone.

entries.pattern: `wonen` is to live somewhere. `leven` is to be alive. Dutch keeps them separate.

examples.nl: Hoe lang woon je hier al?
examples.en: How long have you lived here?

entries.pitfall: Do not use `leven` for your address. `Ik leef in Utrecht` sounds like you are merely surviving there.

entries.pattern: The two most useful words in any language, and a third one: `jawel`, which contradicts a negative.

examples.en: You are not coming, are you? Yes I am!

entries.hook: `jawel` is for arguing back politely. It only exists to answer a question that assumed no.

entries.pattern: A hedge. Buys you time and keeps you from committing to something you are not sure of.
entries.hook: Starting a sentence with misschien pushes the verb to second place: `Misschien kom ik`, not `Misschien ik kom`.
entries.origin: From `mag schien`, 'may happen'. The 'it might happen' is still inside the word.

entries.pattern: A quantity chunk. Also the honest answer to 'do you speak Dutch?'.

examples.en: Could I have a bit of sugar?

entries.hook: `beetje` is the small-and-cute form of `beet`, a bite. A bit is literally a little bite.

entries.pattern: An intensifier pair. `heel erg bedankt` is the warmest everyday thank you.

examples.nl: Het is heel erg koud vandaag.

entries.hook: `erg` on its own means bad, but `heel erg` just means very. Context does the work.

entries.pattern: Two different no-words. `geen` cancels a noun, `niet` cancels everything else.
entries.hook: If you could put `een` or `a` in front of the thing, use `geen`. Otherwise use `niet`.
entries.pitfall: `Ik heb niet tijd` is the single most common beginner error. Nouns take geen.

entries.pattern: A survival sentence. Note that `het` is required: Dutch does not say `ik begrijp niet`.
entries.pitfall: `verstaan` is about hearing, `begrijpen` about meaning. If you simply did not catch it, say `Ik heb u niet verstaan`.

entries.pattern: The polite repair request. Worth knowing by heart before you need it.

examples.en: Could you speak a bit more slowly?

entries.hook: Learn this one before any vocabulary. It buys you a second chance at every sentence you miss.

entries.pattern: `hoeveel` is one word, built from hoe + veel, 'how much'.

examples.en: How many children do you have?

entries.hook: The `hoe` family is worth learning together: hoeveel, hoe laat, hoe lang, hoe ver.

entries.pattern: The question frame you will use most on the street.
A de-word. Nearly every word for a person is a de-word, which is a rare piece of good luck.

examples.nl: De man naast mij is mijn buurman.
examples.en: The man next to me is my neighbour.

entries.hook: People are almost always `de`. That one rule covers a large slice of the nouns you will meet early on.

entries.pattern: A het-word, and irregular in the plural: de kinderen.
entries.hook: `het kind` but `de kinderen`. Every plural is a de-word, so going plural always wipes the problem out.
entries.pitfall: One of the few people-words that is not `de`. Worth marking as an exception now.

entries.pattern: A het-word. The plural softens the s to a z: de huizen.
entries.hook: `thuis` (at home) and `naar huis` (homewards) both hide `huis` inside them.

entries.pattern: A de-word, and the backbone of every time expression you will build.
entries.hook: `vandaag` (today) is literally `van daag`, 'of day'.

entries.pattern: Never learn `elke` alone. It changes shape with het-words (`elk kind`) and the useful thing is the whole time phrase.

examples.nl: Ik fiets elke dag naar mijn werk.
examples.en: I cycle to work every day.

examples.nl: Elke dag een beetje oefenen helpt.
examples.en: Practising a little every day helps.

entries.hook: Swap the noun and you have the whole family: elke week, elke maand, and `elk jaar` because jaar is a het-word.
entries.pitfall: With a het-word it loses the -e: `elk kind`, `elk jaar`. That is why learning the chunk beats learning the word.

entries.pattern: A de-word. Pairs straight into the elke family.
A het-word, and a unit that stays singular after a number.

examples.en: I have lived here for three years.

examples.nl: Elk jaar gaan we naar Spanje.
examples.en: Every year we go to Spain.

entries.hook: Units after a number do not go plural: `drie jaar`, never `drie jaren`.
entries.pitfall: Because it is a het-word it takes `elk jaar`, not `elke jaar`.

packs.title: Everyday things
packs.blurb: The highest-frequency everyday nouns, each stored with its article, plus the fixed phrases they live inside.

entries.pattern: A de-word, and the most Dutch noun there is.
entries.hook: `met de fiets` is the fixed way to say by bike. Transport takes `met`, except on foot, which is `te voet`.

entries.pattern: Transport is always `met de` plus the vehicle. One pattern covers them all.

examples.nl: Ik ga met de trein naar Amsterdam.
examples.en: I go to Amsterdam by train.

examples.nl: Met de bus is het sneller.

entries.hook: Learn the frame, not the nouns: met de trein, met de bus, met de auto, met de fiets.
entries.pitfall: On foot breaks the pattern: `te voet`, with no `met`.

entries.pattern: A het-word. Note that Dutch says you are `op` the station, not `in` it.

examples.en: I am waiting at the station.

entries.hook: `op het station` means inside it. `bij het station` means near it, outside. Arranging to meet with the wrong one leaves you in different places.

entries.pattern: A de-word, and one that takes `-s` in the plural because it ends in an unstressed -el.

examples.nl: De winkel is open tot zes uur.
examples.en: The shop is open until six.

examples.nl: Ik ga even naar de winkel.
examples.en: I am just popping to the shop.

entries.pattern: A fixed verb-plus-noun pair. The noun is always plural and never takes an article here.

examples.en: I am doing the shopping on Saturday.
Have you done the shopping yet?

entries.hook: `boodschap` on its own means a message. Only in the plural, with `doen`, does it mean groceries.
entries.pitfall: Never `de boodschappen doen` with the article in this phrase.

entries.pattern: A de-word. Stress on the first syllable, not the second.

examples.en: Would you like a cup of coffee?

entries.pitfall: Say KOF-fee, not kof-FEE. The English stress pattern marks you out instantly.

entries.pattern: A het-word. The `w` is softer than the English one, closer to a `v`.

examples.en: Could I have a glass of water?

entries.pattern: A het-word. The small form `het broodje` is the roll you buy for lunch.
entries.hook: Every small-and-cute `-je` form is a het-word, so `het broodje` needs no separate memorising.

entries.pattern: A de-word. Shows up in a dozen fixed phrases.
entries.hook: `op tijd` means on time. `de hele tijd` means the whole time. Both are worth having ready-made.

entries.pattern: Literally 'how late is it'. Dutch measures the clock in lateness.

examples.en: What time does the lesson start?

entries.hook: The answer uses `om`: `om acht uur`. Clock times always take om.

entries.pattern: One word, from `van daag`.
entries.hook: Starting with vandaag flips the sentence: `Vandaag ga ik`, not `Vandaag ik ga`.

entries.pattern: Two meanings in one word. Alone it means tomorrow; inside goedemorgen it means morning.

examples.en: Tomorrow morning I have an appointment.

entries.pitfall: `morgenochtend` is tomorrow morning. Plain `morgen` on its own is always tomorrow.

entries.pattern: `straks` is a uniquely useful word: later today, soon, but not now.

examples.en: I will do it in a bit.
Not now, in a little while.

entries.hook: `straks` means later today. `later` can mean any time at all. Dutch people use straks constantly.

entries.pattern: A de-word, from the verb `vragen`.
entries.hook: You `stel` a question in Dutch, you do not ask it: `een vraag stellen`.

entries.pattern: A het-word, and the natural partner to de vraag.

examples.en: I do not know the answer.

entries.hook: Learn `de vraag` and `het antwoord` as a pair, and the opposite articles help you remember both.

entries.pattern: The standard polite request. `graag` is what makes it polite rather than demanding.

examples.nl: Ik wil graag een kopje thee.
examples.en: I would like a cup of tea.

examples.nl: Ik wil graag een afspraak maken.
examples.en: I would like to make an appointment.

entries.hook: Without `graag` it becomes `Ik wil`, which sounds blunt to the point of rude. The word is doing a lot of work.

entries.pattern: The other polite request, slightly softer than `ik wil graag`.
`helpen` takes `met` when you name the thing: `helpen met dit formulier`.

examples.nl: Kunt u mij helpen met dit formulier?
examples.en: Could you help me with this form?

entries.pattern: A de-word, and the hinge of Dutch daily life.

examples.nl: Ik heb een afspraak om drie uur.
examples.en: I have an appointment at three.

entries.hook: You `maak` an appointment in Dutch, you do not take or book one: `een afspraak maken`.

entries.pattern: A fixed verb-plus-noun pair. Opens almost every official phone call you will make.

examples.nl: Ik wil graag een afspraak maken.
examples.en: I would like to make an appointment.

examples.nl: Kan ik vandaag nog een afspraak maken?
examples.en: Could I still make an appointment today?

entries.hook: Learn it as one block with `Ik wil graag` in front. That single sentence opens the doctor, the gemeente and the bank.

entries.pattern: A de-word. The family doctor is `de huisarts`, literally the house-doctor.

examples.en: I am going to the doctor.

examples.nl: Ik ben bij de dokter geweest.
examples.en: I have been to the doctor.

entries.hook: `naar de dokter` for going, `bij de dokter` for being there. The preposition tells you which.

entries.pattern: A de-word. You will be asked for it at every counter in the country.

examples.nl: Mijn naam staat op het formulier.
examples.en: My name is on the form.

entries.pattern: A het-word. Stress falls on the last syllable, unusually for Dutch.

examples.en: I have filled in the form.

entries.hook: You `vul` a form `in`: `invullen` is separable, so `Vul dit formulier in` splits it.

entries.pattern: Worth knowing, and worth using sparingly: most Dutch people will switch to English the moment you ask.

examples.en: I would like to practise Dutch.

entries.hook: Pair it with `Ik wil graag Nederlands oefenen`, or you will never get to practise. Dutch people switch to English out of politeness.
entries.pitfall: Asking this too early ends the Dutch conversation. Try `Kunt u dat herhalen?` first.
